title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single sampled LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic network validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; after preregistered exclusions 266 complete pairs were analysed. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair invoked 6 times; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and therefore the preregistered latency bound could not be evaluated. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We provide preregistered design details, deterministic validator semantics, complete numeric outcomes and contingency counts, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, contamination findings (no exact public duplicates flagged), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and reproducibility artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent‑to‑CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1,2]. Stochastic generation can produce syntactic or semantic violations—missing commands, unsafe command orderings, or constraint breaches—that create operational risk when device CLIs are executed. To mitigate such risk, research and prototype systems interpose deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish or header‑space analyses) and bounded repair loops in generate–verify–repair (GVR) architectures so only verifier‑validated outputs are considered safe to apply [3–5].

Motivated by limited preregistered, paired evaluations that instrument verifier‑triggered repair with archived deterministic traces, we asked the preregistered question: Does a GVR pipeline that uses a single sampled initial model candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), a deterministic Batfish‑style validator, and at most one automated LLM repair call reduce verifier‑detected semantic/safety failures relative to the same initial candidate without repair? Our principal contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation executed under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher constraints that (a) preserves the exact preregistered estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), (b) reports exact paired contingency counts and inferential statistics, and (c) supplies representative validator traces and repair artifacts for audit.
sections.related_work:
Prior NetOps LLM work establishes the promise and failure modes that motivate verifier augmentation. NetConfEval‑style evaluations examine intent→CLI translation and automated configuration synthesis, documenting syntax and sequencing challenges for LLMs in vendor CLI domains [1]. Surveys of LLM applications to intelligent network operations and AIOps review opportunities, typical failure modes (including hallucination and constraint violations), and the need for grounding and verification layers when moving toward automation [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed for deterministic validation in regulated domains and code generation; these proposals motivate pairing a stochastic generator with an external oracle and bounded repair loop [3]. Batfish and related formal/simulation validators provide deterministic reachability and ordering checks that naturally serve as the verification oracle in NetOps pipelines and have been used or proposed in LLM‑augmented prototypes [4]. Investigations of what LLMs need to synthesize correct router configurations emphasize sequence and vendor‑syntax difficulties and thus support verifier‑assisted remediation [5].

Our study differs by executing the preregistered paired estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics, archiving raw model traces and deterministic validator traces, and reporting both exact paired tests and paired bootstrap interval estimates to aid interpretation in small‑discordant samples.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study preregistration is cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under these semantics the same single sampled initial model candidate is used to compute both the baseline outcome (single‑shot candidate → deterministic validator pass/fail) and the guarded outcome (same candidate → verifier; if it fails the guarded arm may invoke at most one automated LLM repair; final verifier pass/fail recorded). This design isolates the effect of the permitted validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial candidate.

Task bank and sampling: The preregistered task bank deterministically produced 300 intent→CLI pairs (150 Cisco‑like; 150 Juniper‑like) using a deterministic synthetic task generator combined with public NetConfEval‑style examples; generation seeds, generator id, and per‑task manifest entries are archived. Inclusion/exclusion, retry, and missingness rules followed the preregistration. Deterministic exclusion logic removed 34 both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures (see analysis/missingness_summary.csv), leaving 266 complete paired units for primary analysis.

Model, orchestration, and sampling settings: The declared model in execution artifacts is gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"); archived fields include max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset). The orchestration adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Provider call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, cache_hit_count = 0, and cache_miss_count = 272. Stage accounting shows shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6. The archived null temperature does not assert deterministic sampling; execution metadata therefore do not exclude nondeterministic sampling by the provider.

Deterministic validator and scoring rule: The verification oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. For each episode the validator performs syntactic CLI parsing and normalization, per‑task required‑sequence checks (expected_sequence vs parsed commands), constrained‑field touch checks (allowed_fields and allowed_touched_fields), and reachability/constraint validation over the synthetic topology. Each episode record archives validation_before and validation_after traces containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, normalized_configuration, and a final binary valid flag. The validator’s binary pass/fail is the primary endpoint and is documented in execution/scoring/*.json artifacts.

Repair loop and shared_initial_candidate mechanics: Per preregistration the initial sampled candidate is shared across baseline and guarded outcomes (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). If the validator fails that candidate, the guarded arm may invoke at most one automated LLM repair call. Repair prompts expose the validator’s failure codes and task constraints and request a corrected configuration; repair prompts and provider traces are archived when invoked. The one‑repair bound was preregistered to model a constrained automated correction stage prior to human escalation.

Analysis plan: The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (α=0.05). For interval estimation we preregistered a paired bootstrap percentile confidence interval (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the paired difference. Secondary estimands included median_repair_iterations_per_task and median end‑to‑end latency (the latter could not be evaluated because per‑episode latency was not archived). Missingness handling followed the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule: pairs with both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures were excluded from the primary test; sensitivity analyses treated excluded pairs conservatively as failures.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and missingness: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68. Complete paired units analysed = 266; both_missing_pairs = 34 were excluded per preregistration (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider and model call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 272, and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (complete_pairs = 266): baseline successes = 260; guarded final successes = 265. Paired contingency counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 260 (both pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed proportions: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015. Paired difference = 0.01879699248. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered α=0.05 decision rule → not significant). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl documents bootstrap parameters and seed).

Repair behavior and representative artifacts: The repair stage executed 6 times across 300 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Representative artifact example: task-000008 (execution/responses/task-000008-shared-initial.txt, sha256 = 89306095ceeedc3df7d752beb035f342edf9e82b7252e45356919e29958245e7) shows the shared initial candidate ending with an incomplete final line ("interface uplink2\n") and produced a validator failure; the guarded final artifact (execution/responses/task-000008-guarded.txt, sha256 = d52b7616f93a608409c7ce4eeb21958b8ceeb502faaf302d9b36468d8a627944) contains the corrected complete sequence and passes validation. All episode validator traces for this task (execution/scoring/task-000008-*.json) archive concrete failure codes that triggered the repair and the normalized_configuration accepted after repair. analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no exact public‑duplicate flags for primary analysis items.

Sensitivity checks: Treating the 34 excluded both‑arm episodes as failures (conservative N=300 analysis) yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333 but leaves discordant counts unchanged (n10=5, n01=0) and exact McNemar p = 0.0625; thus the primary inferential null decision is robust to the preregistered conservative missingness handling.

Supplementary archived quantitative artifacts: condition_summary.csv and paired_contingency_table.csv are archived (SHA‑256 values in analysis artifact hashes). deterministic_reconciliation.json verifies that deterministic consistency checks passed and provides provider call and stage counts used above.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The guarded GVR pipeline produced a small absolute increase in validator pass‑rate (~1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI that narrowly excludes zero illustrates a known finite‑sample phenomenon: exact McNemar depends only on discrete discordant counts (here n10=5, n01=0) producing a discrete p‑value, while the bootstrap CI reflects empirical paired‑difference variability and can exclude zero in small‑discordant settings. Reporting both inferential perspectives allows balanced judgment about practical relevance versus formal hypothesis acceptance.

Operational implications and boundary conditions: The marginal benefit of the bounded automated repair was limited because baseline single‑shot pass rate was already high (≈97.7%), leaving few failures for repair to correct; repair invocations were rare (6/300). For workloads with high first‑pass accuracy, the operational ROI of adding an automated bounded repair stage may be small. Conversely, GVR is likely to show larger absolute gains when first‑pass accuracy is lower or when the validator’s rule coverage expands to detect additional classes of semantic error.

Threats to validity and concrete artifact evidence: Internal validity: our shared_initial_candidate estimand measures the effect of validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent multiple draws or constrained first‑pass prompting (those alternatives were not executed and are outside the estimand). Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite battery of syntactic, required‑sequence, and reachability rules; semantic violations outside its rule set remain undetected and unmeasured—this is explicit in each episode’s validator_trace fields archived in execution/scoring/*.json. External validity: the task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor dialect clusters; generalization to additional vendor CLIs, larger production topologies, or different task difficulty distributions is not supported by these artifacts. Conclusion validity: few discordant pairs (n10=5, n01=0) and the loss of 34 provider‑failure pairs reduced power and precision; deterministic_reconciliation.json documents these counts and provider call failures.

Design lessons grounded in artifacts: (1) For high baseline pass‑rate workloads, design experiments on lower‑baseline corpora to improve power to detect repair benefits. (2) Archive per‑episode latency and pipeline timing (not present here) to evaluate preregistered operational bounds—the absence of latency fields in execution artifacts prevented evaluation of the preregistered latency estimand. (3) Expand and publicly document validator rule coverage so that construct‑validity gaps can be measured (episode validator_trace shows the specific violation codes and normalized_configuration for diagnostics). (4) Consider additional preregistered arms (e.g., independent second draws or constrained‑prompting arms) if the goal is to compare generation strategies rather than the effect of a validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample.
sections.conclusion: A preregistered paired experiment evaluated a bounded GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) on intent→CLI tasks under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved validator pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be assessed. All execution and analysis artifacts, including raw responses, validator traces, provider call accounting, and reconciliation manifests, are archived in the evidence bundle to support reanalysis and follow‑on work. The results indicate that when first‑pass generator accuracy is high, bounded automated repair yields limited absolute gains; future work should evaluate lower‑baseline corpora, record latency, and expand deterministic verifier coverage to measure broader semantic safety improvements.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure: Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json archived; declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration: cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Initial master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: before the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the autonomy lock the registered pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, preregistration, experimental execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review simulation, and revision. Nondeterminism disclosure: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) and no deterministic sampling seed is archived; therefore nondeterministic sampling of model outputs cannot be excluded for the recorded provider calls. Execution and analysis artifacts, logs, and hash manifests referenced in the preregistration are archived in the evidence bundle for audit per the track’s reproducibility requirements.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
